''Lepidium draba'', commonly known as '''hoary cress''', '''whitetop''', '''whiteweed''', or '''peppergrass''', is a [[perennial]] plant species in the mustard family, [[Brassicaceae]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Whitetop {{!}} National Invasive Species Information Center |url=https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/terrestrial/plants/whitetop |access-date=2026-04-18 |website=www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Gaskin |first1=John F. |last2=Zhang |first2=Dao-Yuan |last3=Bon |first3=Marie-Claude |date=March 20, 2026 |title=Invasion of Lepidium draba (Brassicaceae) in the western United States: distributions and origins of chloroplast DNA haplotypes |journal=Molecular Ecology |volume=14 |issue=8 |pages=2331–2341 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-294X.2005.02589.x |issn=0962-1083 |pmid=15969718}}</ref> It is native to [[Eurasia]], specifically regions of [[Europe]] and western to [[central Asia]], but has become widely distributed across the globe.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Zouhar |first=Kris |date=April 17, 2026 |title=Cardaria spp. In: Fire Effects Information System |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/forb/carspp3/all.html#OTHER%20STATUS |access-date=2026-04-18 |website=www.fs.usda.gov}}</ref> The species was first recorded in the [[United States]] around 1862, believed to have been unintentionally introduced through contaminated agricultural seed or [[ship ballast]].<ref name=":2" /> Since then, it has been found throughout most of the United States, as well as in [[Canada]] and parts of [[Mexico]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Cripps |first=Michael |date=November 23, 2006 |title=Comparative survey of the phytophagous arthropod faunas associated with Lepidium draba in Europe and the western United States, and the potential for biological weed control |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/09583150600828361 |access-date=2026-04-18 |journal=Biocontrol Science and Technology |volume=16 |issue=10 |pages=1007–1030 |doi=10.1080/09583150600828361 |bibcode=2006BioST..16.1007C |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Heart-podded Hoary Cress.jpg|thumb|Typically each flower has four petals|left|249x249px]]Whitetop is a perennial herb that reproduces by seeds and by horizontal creeping roots.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lepidium draba Profile – California Invasive Plant Council |url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/plants/profile/cardaria-draba-profile/ |access-date=2023-06-17 |language=en-US}}</ref> The stem is stoutish, erect or spreading, 10 to 80 cm tall, branched, covered sparsely with grayish, soft hairs.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board |url=https://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weeds/hoary-cress |access-date=2026-04-18 |website=www.nwcb.wa.gov}}</ref> The leaves are alternate, simple, and mostly toothed. Basal leaves measure 4-10 cm in length, have short petioles, and are lanceolate to ovate in shape.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Scurfield |first=G. |date=July 1962 |title=Cardaria Draba (L.) Desv. |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/2257459 |journal=The Journal of Ecology |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=489–499 |doi=10.2307/2257459 |jstor=2257459 |bibcode=1962JEcol..50..489S |issn=0022-0477|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Upper stem leaves are sessile, 2-6.5 cm long, and [[Glossary of leaf morphology|oblong]] to [[Glossary of leaf morphology|tapering]], with broad bases that clasp the stem.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hoary cress (Cardaria draba) |url=https://agri.nv.gov/Plant/Noxious_Weeds/WeedList/Hoary_cress_(Cardaria_draba)/ |access-date=2023-06-17 |website=agri.nv.gov}}</ref> 

The plant produces slightly domed, [[corymb]]-like clusters of white flowers, in which the individual flower stalks grow upward from various points off the branch to approximately the same height. 

=== Flowering ===
Flowering usually occurs in the spring to early summer. Each flower typically has four white petals measuring 3-5 mm in length, approximately twice as long as the [[sepal]]s.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=MULLIGAN |first1=GERALD A. |last2=FINDLAY |first2=JUDY N. |date=January 1974 |title=The biology of canadian weeds. 3. cardaria draba, c. chalepensis, and c. pubescens |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=149–160 |doi=10.4141/cjps74-024 |issn=0008-4220|doi-access=free |bibcode=1974CJPlS..54..149M }}</ref> After flowering, the plant forms heart-shaped seed pods called silicles, each containing two seeds.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Lepidium draba (heart-podded pepperweed): Go Botany |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/lepidium/draba/ |access-date=2026-04-18 |website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org}}</ref>
[[File:Korina 2016-05-26 Lepidium draba 3.jpg|thumb|395x395px|Dense, flat-topped corymbs of ''L. draba'' during blooming period in the spring to early summer<ref name=":3" />]]

== Distribution ==
[[Image:Cardaria-draba-distribution-USDA.png|thumb|334x334px|Distribution map of ''L. draba'' in the United States ]]''Lepidium draba'' has become widely distributed beyond its native range. In North America, it is now found throughout most of the United States, particularly in the central and western regions, as well as in Canada and parts of Mexico.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /> It has been suggested that native grasses from the ''[[Poa]]'' genera may be able to outcompete whitetop in North America.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Puliafico |first1=Kenneth P. |last2=Schwarzländer |first2=Mark |last3=Price |first3=William J. |last4=Harmon |first4=Bradley L. |last5=Hinz |first5=Hariet L. |date=March 2011 |title=Native and Exotic Grass Competition with Invasive Hoary Cress (Cardaria draba) |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/invasive-plant-science-and-management/article/abs/native-and-exotic-grass-competition-with-invasive-hoary-cress-cardaria-draba/A4D6E9CABA2E1BEB835BFFEC1FB69EE3#access-block |journal=Invasive Plant Science and Management |language=en |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=38–49 |doi=10.1614/IPSM-D-10-00041.1 |bibcode=2011IPSM....4...38P |s2cid=85677227 |issn=1939-7291|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A distribution map demonstrates its spread across North America. 

== Behavior ==

=== Reproduction ===
''Lepidium draba'' reproduces through both clonal (vegetative) and sexual (seed-based) methods, with clonal reproduction being the dominant method.<ref name=":2" /> The plant spreads via lateral [[Rhizome|rhizomes]], allowing it to expand rapidly and form dense, interconnected patches.<ref name=":4" /> Individual plants can produce hundreds of new shoots each year, contributing to the formation of large, long-lived colonies.<ref name=":4" /> This clonal growth allows the plant to persist even under abnormal conditions, as it can regenerate easily from root fragments, especially after [[Disturbance (ecology)|disturbance]].<ref name=":4" />

In addition, ''L. draba'' produces seeds in large quantities through [[sexual reproduction]]. A single shoot can produce hundreds of seed pods, each containing two seeds.<ref name=":5" /> These seeds can remain viable in the soil for several years and [[Germination|germinate]] in the spring and fall.<ref name=":4" /> While seed production plays a smaller role in local population expansion, it is important for long-distance dispersal and the establishment of new populations. As a result, these reproductive methods make ''L. draba'' highly resilient and difficult to control. 

=== Invasiveness ===
Today, ''Lepidium draba'' is recognized as a [[Noxious weed|noxious]] weed and as an invasive species in many areas due to its ability to thrive in [[Disturbance (ecology)|disturbed areas]] such as agricultural fields, roadsides, and [[Rangeland|rangelands]], where it spreads rapidly and dominates native plant species.<ref name=":4" /> Its invasiveness is also due to its extensive rhizomatous root system, which allows the plant to spread rapidly through clonal expansion and form dense, persistent patches and expand several meters per year without relying on seed production.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /> Additionally, the plant can regenerate from small root fragments and is highly resistant to mechanical and chemical control methods.<ref name=":4" /> 
[[File:Lepidium draba 2.jpg|thumb|408x408px|''L. draba'' forming a dense monoculture in a disturbed field]]
Although clonal reproduction is dominant, human activities have played a significant role in its spread, particularly through the movement of contaminated agricultural seeds such as [[alfalfa]].<ref name=":2" /> Once established, the plant continues to spread unintentionally through agricultural practices and in disturbed environments, including agricultural systems and [[Riparian zone|riparian zones]], where it outcompetes native plants.<ref name=":4" /> Its high environmental tolerance further supports its persistence and success as an invasive species across a wide range of conditions.<ref name=":4" />

In addition, the plant may show [[Allelopathy|allelopathic]] effects by releasing chemical compounds that prevent the growth of surrounding plant species and reduce competition.<ref name=":4" /> Its persistence, rapid spread, and adaptability allow it to outcompete those that are native to the environment and dominate invaded ecosystems, making it a significant ecological concern. 

=== Ecological Impact ===
The ecological impacts ''L. draba'' has in the regions it invades are significant. It reduces [[biodiversity]] by outcompeting native plant species, which leads to simplified plant communities and disrupted [[Ecosystem|ecosystems]].<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Gaskin |first=John F. |date=March 27, 2026 |title=Clonal structure of invasive hoary cress (Lepidium draba) infestations |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/weed-science/article/abs/clonal-structure-of-invasive-hoary-cress-lepidium-draba-infestations/B423A8BCDAE7C5CC6D527A2D00C2F640 |journal=Weed Science |language=en |volume=54 |issue=3 |pages=428–434 |doi=10.1614/WS-05-138R.1 |issn=0043-1745|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This can affect organisms that depend on those plants for food and habitat. 

In addition to its ecological effects, it negatively impacts agricultural systems. It can reduce [[crop]] yields and [[forage]] quality in [[Pasture|pastures]], making it problematic for farmers and land managers.<ref name=":1" /> The plant also serves as a host for various agricultural pests, specifically for those that affect crops within the Brassicaceae, which can potentially increase pest pressure in nearby cultivated fields.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":6" />

Moreover, ''L. draba'' contains chemical compounds known as [[Glucosinolate|glucosinolates]], which can be toxic to [[livestock]] if consumed in large quantities.<ref name=":4" /> These compounds may also contribute to its ability to interfere with surrounding plant growth. 

== Ecology and Competition ==
''Lepidium draba'' is a highly competitive, disturbance‑adapted perennial whose success is driven by vigorous clonal growth, deep root reserves, and potent chemical defenses that suppress neighboring vegetation.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=Hinz |first=Hariet L. |last2=Schwarzländer |first2=Mark |last3=McKenney |first3=Jessica L. |last4=Cripps |first4=Michael G. |last5=Harmon |first5=Bradley |last6=Price |first6=William J. |date=2012-10-01 |title=Biogeographical comparison of the invasive Lepidium draba in its native, expanded and introduced ranges |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10530-012-0207-z |journal=Biological Invasions |language=en |volume=14 |issue=10 |pages=1999–2016 |doi=10.1007/s10530-012-0207-z |issn=1573-1464|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Its ability to rapidly colonize disturbed soils allows it to dominate plant communities and outcompete both native and agricultural species.<ref name=":8" /> Genetic analyses from both native Eurasian populations and introduced North American populations reveal unexpectedly high [[genetic diversity]], indicating that the species experienced multiple introduction events rather than a single [[founder effect]] or [[Population bottleneck|genetic bottleneck]]. This broad genetic base likely enhances its ecological flexibility and contributes to its strong competitiveness.<ref name=":8" /> 
[[File:Korina 2011-05-12 Lepidium draba.jpg|thumb|345x345px|Monocultures of ''L. draba'' infesting a roadside]]
Generally, the plant thrives in disturbed, nutrient‑rich, and open habitats such as agricultural fields, roadsides, and abandoned lands, where reduced competition enables rapid establishment and spread.<ref name=":8" /> Its high seed production and efficient dispersal mechanisms allow it to colonize new sites quickly, reinforcing its invasive expansion across landscapes.<ref name=":8" /> In competitive settings, ''L. draba'' exerts strong dominance over native grasses and [[Forb|forbs]], significantly reducing their biomass and recruitment when grown together. European plant species tend to show greater tolerance to the chemical and physical interference exerted by ''L. draba'', suggesting that coevolution in its native range moderates its competitive impact. Overall, the species’ ecological success is driven by its ability to exploit [[Disturbance (ecology)|disturbance]], suppress neighbors, and rapidly occupy available space.<ref name=":8" />

In reference to its primary characteristics, its ability to spread aggressively through underground [[Rhizome|rhizomes]] allows it to dominate disturbed and semi-natural [[Habitat|habitats]] where [[Competition (biology)|competition]] is reduced.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last=McKenney |first=Jessica L. |last2=Cripps |first2=Michael G. |last3=Price |first3=William J. |last4=Hinz |first4=Hariet L. |last5=Schwarzländer |first5=Mark |date=2007 |title=No Difference in Competitive Ability between Invasive North American and Native European Lepidium draba Populations |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/40212995 |journal=Plant Ecology |volume=193 |issue=2 |pages=293–303 |issn=1385-0237}}</ref> This vegetative growth strategy allows the plant to rapidly occupy space and suppress neighboring vegetation, contributing to its ecological success.<ref name=":9" /> Interestingly, comparative studies show no significant difference in competitive ability between invasive North American populations and native European populations, suggesting that its dominance is not solely a product of novel environmental conditions but rather an inherent trait of the species across its range.

== Control ==
[[File:Ceutorrhynchus assimilis (31943140745).jpg|thumb|287x287px|The cabbage weevil (''[[Ceutorhynchus]] assimilis)'' as a potential biological agent against ''L. draba<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fumanal |first1=Boris |last2=Martin |first2=Jean-François |last3=Sobhian |first3=Rouhollah |last4=Blanchet |first4=Arnaud |last5=Bon |first5=Marie-Claude |date=2004-07-01 |title=Host range of Ceutorhynchus assimilis (Coleoptera: Curculionidae), a candidate for biological control of Lepidium draba (Brassicaceae) in the USA |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1049964404000337 |journal=Biological Control |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=598–607 |doi=10.1016/j.biocontrol.2004.03.001 |bibcode=2004BiolC..30..598F |issn=1049-9644|url-access=subscription }}</ref>'']]
''Lepidium draba'' presents significant challenges for control and eradication due to its clonal growth and regenerative capacity.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Goodwin |first=Kim |date=April 19, 2026 |title=Biology, Ecology and Management of Whitetop |url=https://www.montana.edu/extension/invasiveplants/documents/publications/extension_publications/whitetop.pdf |url-status=live |access-date=April 19, 2026}}</ref> Its underground [[Rhizome|rhizomes]] make physical removal difficult, and even small root fragments can regenerate into new plants, allowing populations to persist and reestablish after disturbance.<ref name=":10" /> The species is notably resistant to [[Herbicide|herbicides]], [[grazing]], and manual removal, further complicating management efforts.<ref name=":8" /> To prevent its spread, it is essential to clean equipment, vehicles, and personal gear after working in infested areas to avoid unintentionally transporting plant material.<ref name=":10" /> Long-term suppression strategies include the use of host-specific [[Biological pest control|biological control agents]], such as root-feeding and stem-mining [[Weevil|weevils]], which gradually weaken the plant.<ref name=":8" /> Additionally, systemic herbicides applied in early spring or fall can reduce root reserves, though repeated treatments over multiple years are necessary for a meaningful impact.<ref name=":10" />

== Ongoing Research ==
Recent research on ''L. draba'' has spanned across ecology, physiology, and biomedical science. This has been researched for both its invasive traits and its medical potential.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |last1=Karan |first1=Tunay |last2=Cadirci |first2=Bilge Hilal |date=June 28, 2018 |title=EVALUATION OF ANTIMICROBIAL AND ANTIOXIDANT ACTIVITY OF LEPIDIUM DRABA L. |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/326155280 |website=[[ResearchGate]]}}</ref> Ecological work finds that its seeds have strong [[drought]] tolerance and chemical dormancy, helping the plant spread in dry environments.  Researchers have reported that L. draba extracts can protect the liver, kidneys, and intestines. In [[biotechnology]], researchers have improved the stability and efficiency of L. draba [[peroxidase]] enzymes by attaching them to [[Magnetic nanoparticles in drug delivery|magnetic nanoparticles]].<ref name=":7" />
